title: AR Rahman on Ramayana: Two Themes Each With Hans Zimmer, and No Rush to Judge
excerpt: The composer defends months of work behind Mangal Rang, explains how he and Hans Zimmer split the score, and talks about still getting nervous on stage.
body:
• AR Rahman is composing the music for Nitesh Tiwari's Hindi film Ramayana alongside Hans Zimmer, with each composer developing his own themes and Rahman writing the songs with lyricist Kumar Vishwas.
  • Responding to criticism of the song Mangal Rang, Rahman said his compositions are lived with for months: "I am my first critic. It is not that I just love everything I do."
  • The film stars Ranbir Kapoor as Ram, Sai Pallavi as Sita and Yash as Ravana, and is set for release on November 5, according to the coverage.
  • Rahman said Zimmer's involvement could bring new audiences to a story that holds a significant place in the cultural imagination of the Indian subcontinent.

AR Rahman is composing for the epic he first met as a child. In interviews with The Indian Express group's Indulge, the composer described returning to the Ramayana through Nitesh Tiwari's Hindi film Ramayana — and the question he asked himself when he saw the scale of director Nitesh Tiwari and producer Namit Malhotra's vision: what else can he bring to the table?

"I think, from childhood, from school annual functions where Ramayana was performed as a play, to watching musical theatre in Tamil Nadu, RS Manohar's dramas on stage, TV series and movies, you question yourself: what else can I bring to the table? So, when I saw the vision of Nitesh Tiwari and Namit Malhotra, I was blown away by the ambition and the relentless work they've been putting in," Rahman said. Seeing the film in 3D, he added, was "dazzling and quite breathtaking."

Two composers, one epic

Rahman is creating the music alongside German composer Hans Zimmer. Asked how the two divide the work, Rahman said there is no turf war: "Hans developed a couple of themes, and I developed a couple of themes, and they all have their place in the movie. There is a lot of respect among all the teams, and this makes the collaboration more special."

The songs fell to Rahman, working with lyricist Kumar Vishwas. "It's exciting because he has so much information and such ease with the vocabulary of that era. I keep telling him that every cell of his is filled with these words," Rahman said. "It was a great honour to work with Kumar Vishwas as a lyricist because I've worked with many lyricists in India, and this was very different." Rahman has also said Zimmer's involvement could bring new audiences to the story.

"Hans developed a couple of themes, and I developed a couple of themes, and they all have their place in the movie."

— AR Rahman, composer

Answering the Mangal Rang criticism

The music has not arrived without argument. Mangal Rang, a song from the film featuring Ranbir Kapoor, Sai Pallavi and Yash, drew criticism on social media after its release, with some listeners describing a qawwali-like treatment, objecting to the electronic treatment of the Ravana tandava and questioning Kumar Vishwas's lyrics, according to coverage of the Indian Express interview.

Rahman's answer was that the work is slower and more deliberate than the reaction cycle. "I am my first critic. It is not that I just love everything I do," he said. "We don't decide something in a day. We live with it for months sometimes. There's a thought process. Sometimes you need to take anthropology into consideration." Listeners, he added, sometimes see only one aspect of a composition and need time to understand the choices behind it. For Mangal Rang, he said he drew on the shuddh notes of Bilawal, with elements of Maand and Pahadi, intending the composition to draw from familiar devotional musical traditions. The film's songs have been reported as appearing in five languages.

A nervous performer, and a full slate

For all the accolades, the interviews also covered why Rahman still gets nervous before performing live — a reminder that the studio perfectionist and the stage performer are the same person approaching the work from opposite ends. He is also stepping in front of the camera: Moonwalk, a dance-musical comedy directed by Manoj NS and headlined by Prabhu Deva, marks his first real acting role, an experience he described as natural after years of directing and being filmed himself.

Ramayana stars Ranbir Kapoor as Ram, Sai Pallavi as Sita and Yash as Ravana, and is set to release on November 5. Rahman's upcoming projects, as reported alongside the interview, include Ramayana: Part 2, Shekhar Kapur's Masoom: The Next Generation and Mani Ratnam's Inji Vellam. For diaspora audiences who grew up with both the epic and Rahman's music, the pairing of the two — with Zimmer alongside — is the draw: a story almost every Indian knows, scored by the composer many of them grew up hearing.
